title: Employment Rights: Salary, Contracts and Harassment
summary: Appointment letters, notice periods, unpaid salary, workplace harassment, PF and gratuity.
sectionRefs: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013

body.text: If you have worked, you must be paid, on time and in full. Indian law also protects you on contracts, notice, leave and harassment. Knowing the basics helps you act instead of worry.

items: Read the appointment letter: salary, working hours, notice period, leave and termination clauses.
Keep a signed copy. If something is promised verbally, ask for it in writing.
Deductions must have a legal basis. Arbitrary cuts can be challenged before the labour authorities.
Wages must be paid by the agreed date; for many workers, within 7 to 10 days of the wage period.
Keep your payslips and bank statements; they are your proof of what was due and paid.
An employer cannot withhold your full and final settlement without a lawful reason.
A notice period is what your contract or the law requires; both sides should honour it.
You can resign. The employer must still pay you for the days you worked.
Termination must follow the contract and the law. Being sacked in revenge for raising a complaint can be challenged.
Leave is governed by your contract and the applicable labour law.
Sexual harassment at the workplace is prohibited. Workplaces above a threshold must have an Internal Committee.
You can complain to the Internal Committee, or to the Local Committee for smaller workplaces.
Provident Fund (PF) contributions by the employer are mandatory for covered establishments.
Gratuity is generally payable after five years of continuous service in covered cases.
ESI and other benefits apply where the establishment is covered.

body.text: Never sign a resignation or settlement letter you do not understand. Signing may reduce your claim.
Keep your appointment letter, payslips, attendance records, bank statements and any written promises. These are your proof.
For unpaid salary, you can file a complaint with the Labour Commissioner or apply for recovery of the money due. For PF, complain to the EPFO.

practicalSteps: Collect your appointment letter, payslips, attendance records and bank statements.
Send a polite written demand and keep a copy.
File a complaint with the Labour Commissioner or the labour court.
For PF issues, complain to the EPFO; for harassment, approach the Internal or Local Committee.
For unpaid salary, an application can be filed for recovery of the money due.
exceptions: Some categories of workers and very small establishments have different thresholds under the law.
Certain higher-earning employees may not be covered by parts of the wage laws, but contract terms and general law still apply.

faqs.q: Can my employer cut my salary as punishment?
faqs.a: Only lawful deductions are allowed. Punitive deductions without a legal basis can be challenged before the labour authorities.

faqs.q: What about my PF and gratuity?
faqs.a: Employer contributions to PF are mandatory for covered establishments. Gratuity is payable after five years of continuous service in covered cases.

misconceptions.myth: If I complain, I will surely lose my job.
misconceptions.fact: Retaliation is unlawful, and complaints can be made to the labour authorities. Legal aid services and labour unions can support you.
